blocks.text: A record 1.57 million international passengers arrived at Cape Town International in FY25/26, against 1.16 million in FY19/20, before the pandemic (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25; the same series stood at 1.44 million in FY24/25; Wesgro Research, Western Cape Tourism Performance: Annual 2025; Wesgro, presentation to the parliamentary committee, 1 Apr 2026; on South African Tourism's provincial count the province received 1,538,142 in 2025, still below the 2 million of 2019, and the two series count different things, as section 1.1 sets out). Its average load factor of 79% in 2025 was the joint highest of South Africa's five largest airports, with Lanseria (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The South African Market"). Between 2015 and 2025 the airport added 17 mainline international routes, more than any of eight peer airports (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"). On the airport count, the recovery is complete. The next stage is harder, because the system that delivered it is now full at the peak.

Interest is not what holds the province back. About 97 million high-value travellers in 34 markets are interested in South Africa, yet only about one in seventy of them, some 1.4 million, turns that interest into a trip (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p41). Seats and bookings stand in the way. Eleven of 27 international routes run above 80% load across the year, and at the summer peak one runway caps movements at about 30 an hour (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101). In winter, carriers pull seats: June holds 6.4% of the year's international capacity, against 10.8% in December (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Beyond the Metro, most rural properties are missing from the online travel agents where visitors book (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p95).

On the growth model's count, arrivals can grow from about 1.5 million in 2025 to 2.5 million by 2035, if the province wins the seats (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20; the model and the airport series count arrivals differently, as section 1.1 sets out). That makes this strategy a supply programme before it is a marketing programme.
The province earns a premium from a narrow base

The Western Cape earns more per visitor than the rest of South Africa. The province takes about a quarter of national foreign spend from about a seventh of the arrivals. Its foreign visitors spend roughly 1.6 times the national average (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11; computed). That is about US$890 per arrival, against US$500 for the rest of South Africa (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p15). Foreign direct spend rose 14% in a year, from R22.7bn in FY2024 to R25.9bn in FY2025 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11).

Yet the premium rests on a few markets, six months and one metro. Five markets supply 63% of overseas arrivals, and the UK, Germany and the USA alone 52% (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p13). More than half the arrivals on the ten largest routes come through someone else's hub: the routes through Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa and Istanbul carry 53% of them (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p13; computed). October to March carries between 61% and 62% of overseas visitor travel (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25, p32; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12; the 2025 shares are provisional and scaled to 100%). The Cape Metro holds 20,281 of the province's 50,332 tourism assets, or 40.3%, and visitors disperse from there (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p2, p22, p23). Growth now needs new markets, new seasons and new regions.
The limits are physical and institutional
Five constraints cap the case, and none of them is a lack of interest in the province.

**The gateway.** The growth model draws air access as a line at 1.8 million inbound seats, and the base path crosses it around 2030 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). The line is the model's assumption, not a measured cap. In practice the runway binds first, at peak hours. Runway relief comes from about 2033 (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101 to p103). Airports Company South Africa (ACSA) now schedules the realigned runway for December 2029, subject to contract award (ACSA, Q1 2026/27 presentation to the Portfolio Committee on Transport, as reported by Travel News, Aug 2026). This strategy plans on about 2033 and counts the earlier date as upside. George Airport is domestic only, and Cape Winelands Airport targets 2028 with no named carrier (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p104 to p109).

**Full routes.** Five of the eleven full routes are mature long-haul services, led by Newark at 88.6%, Atlanta at 84.3% and Frankfurt and London Heathrow at 83.0% (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). On full routes, carriers are expected to raise fares before they add seats (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "In Conclusion").

**Seasons.** The green season, April to September, is a seat problem and a demand problem at once: seats and visitors fall away together. Connecting traffic is "especially critical in the low season" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary"). That ties winter seats to the hub carriers' own priorities.

**Reach.** Accessibility falls from 4.7 out of 5 in the Cape Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo, and one touring route of six is rated Ready. Beyond the Metro and the Garden Route the province is effectively car-only (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88 to p90, p30, p99).

**Levers held elsewhere.** National government and its state-owned entities hold visas, air service agreements and the airport and port programmes (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p103, p112). Mobility mandates are split across three tiers, and no approved method exists for provincial tourism GDP and jobs (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p23, p37).
Most of the five sit outside a marketing budget, and the runway and air rights sit outside the province.
What 2.5 million arrivals would take

Wesgro's original ask was larger: a strategy to "double international tourist arrivals to the Western Cape by 2035" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p4). The evidence reframes that ambition as growth to 2.5 million. The province's Growth for Jobs Strategy sets 3 million by 2035 on South African Tourism's count (Wesgro, presentation to the parliamentary committee, 1 Apr 2026; public source). That sits above every path the growth model draws, and section 1.1 explains why the two cannot yet be compared directly. [G4J 2023 document to be read and the 3 million target confirmed against it.]

The gateway sets the pace in the summer peak, and demand and conversion set it in the green season and beyond the Metro. The growth model draws three paths from a 2025 base of about 1.5 million (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20). By 2035 the conservative path reaches about 1.8 million, the base path about 2.2 million and the accelerated path about 2.5 million. Chapters 1 to 5 call the last two the base and accelerated cases.

The paths differ by intervention, not by demand potential. The base path assumes Wesgro holds its current effort while Emirates, Qatar, Ethiopian and Turkish Airlines keep adding capacity. The accelerated path also needs direct India and China routes and dedicated activation in India, China, the USA and the Gulf. Without confirmed routes, it reverts to base (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p19, p20).

On the eleven full routes, marketing cannot make up for missing seats, but on the hub routes, at 65% to 72% load, it can (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "In Conclusion", "Seasonality"). The hub markets supply about 30% of the arrivals the base path adds, the largest share of any market group (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19, p20; computed).

The base path implies growth of 3.8% a year and the accelerated path 5.3%, against a global norm of 3% to 5% (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p7). Faster growth has been sustained without a recovery tailwind. Valencia ended 2024 24.4% above 2019, and Santiago's airport grew from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p46, p24, p25). The fastest growers aimed institutions, marketing and air access at one binding constraint (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p58, p59). For Chile that constraint was long-haul access. The Western Cape's constraint has the same shape: seats into one gateway airport.
The strategy makes three shifts

In Pillar 1, Reshape demand, the work moves from awareness to conversion. The province is under-sold in its growth markets and hard to book outside its core. Three of its six focus areas aim at conversion: green-season events, bookable product and hub traffic already in the air. About 101,000 Indian and Chinese travellers a year already reach Cape Town, mainly through Gulf and African hubs (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p46, p48; computed). Singapore shows how a hub can turn transit into visits, and Melbourne uses its events calendar to steady demand (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p18, p40, p59).

In Pillar 2, Transform supply, the work moves from new attractions to seats and finished experiences. The pillar has one capacity entry: frequency and larger aircraft on the full routes ahead of runway relief. Following Chile, Initiative I6 designs a public-private air access fund in 2027 and 2028 to back it (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28; section 4.3). Five more cover cruise, reach, product and experience. Cruise grows through ships and excursions rather than port capital (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112). At the flagship sites the task is to manage flows, because Boulders is near carrying capacity and Cableway queues run up to three hours (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24, p36). Elsewhere it is to turn existing assets into complete visitor experiences (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p114).

In Pillar 3, Build enabling capability, the work moves from separate mandates to shared decisions, capital and data. The pillar answers four questions. First, who benefits: twenty township and rural communities hold 18.4% of the province's residents, but the spend traced to them is a floor of 0.02% to 0.04% of foreign direct spend (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5). Second, who pays: the capital pipeline funds airports, ports, roads and rail, but almost none of it reaches the beds, booking and product the regions lack (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p32 to p87, p100, p112). Third, who decides: with visas and air service agreements held nationally, the province leads by escalation (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). Fourth, who measures: more than twenty bodies produce tourism data, yet no one holds a single view of visitor behaviour (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p56, p57). The New Zealand case argues for yield over arrivals, so the plan tracks spend, season and spread beside arrivals (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p55, p56; section 5.3).
The three pillars make one case. Demand work fills seats only if the seats exist, and supply work pays only if the product can be booked. Both need the enabling base to last.
Twenty focus areas at a glance
The twenty focus areas come from testing the December 2025 hypothesis tree against the evidence. Ten carried through as Validated and none was withdrawn (section 1.4).
Each table gives a focus area's disposition, its Chapter 3 finding word for word and its initiative.
Seats and bookings move first

Air access and bookability move first, because every other lever runs through them. The plan runs in three phases. Activate, from 2027 to 2028, holds and adds seats on the full routes, counts the bookability gap and sets up the institutions the rest depends on. Gate 1 closes the phase at the end of 2028, two years before the base path crosses the seat line (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). Expand, from 2029 to 2031, scales what works and meets the seat line at the 2030 mid-term review. Sustain, from 2032 to 2035, takes direct route cases to carriers as runway capacity arrives.

Eighteen initiatives carry the plan, one per focus area except where one owner delivers two. Wesgro is accountable for twelve. The Department of Economic Development and Tourism (DEDAT), the Department of Mobility, municipalities, local tourism organisations (LTOs) and site operators lead the other six. Thirteen draw mainly on Wesgro's operating budget. None has yet been costed, and setting the rand bands is the first funding task (section 4.6).
Twelve actions in three strands can start in the first 24 months, nine of them inside Wesgro's current mandate and budget.

Seats and season come first, from the first half of 2027. Cape Town Air Access holds winter seats through joint marketing with carriers on the full routes and tracks the runway quarterly (I6, I2). The Convention Bureau publishes a green-season events calendar and aims bids at May to September (I2).

Governance and baselines also start then. The Wesgro CEO's office and DEDAT constitute the Tourism Growth Steerco and table the first national escalation agenda (I15, I17). Wesgro's Research unit agrees a data-sharing protocol with ACSA, SA Tourism, Stats SA and Cape Town Tourism (I16). It also runs a bookability census by district and requests visitor counts from the five flagship sites (I3, I11).

Product and inclusion follow in the second half of 2027. Wesgro's Tourism unit packages the Garden Route and Route 62 with a shuttle transfer (I8, I9). It also packages the Southern Line as a visitor product with the City of Cape Town and the Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa (I8). It chooses two or three pilot communities, and from the first half of 2028 the LTOs give each community one live booking route before any promotion (I12, I3). Each action opens a seat, a baseline or a booking path a later initiative needs. Owners and start dates are proposals for Steerco to confirm (section 4.5).
How the Board will track progress

The Board will judge the plan on seven impact indicators, and today only arrivals and spend carry a modelled value for 2035. Beneath them sit twenty-five outcome and thirty-six output indicators. Steerco receives a quarterly scorecard and the Board an annual outlook against both paths. Gates at the end of 2028 and 2031, a mid-term review in 2030 and a terminal evaluation in 2035 decide what each phase funds.

The table shows the model's arrivals baseline, and the airport count is tracked beside it, from 1.44 million in FY24/25 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11; section 5.3). The spend target needs the same care. The model's 2024 spend of R27.12bn sits 19% above the R22.7bn reported for FY2024, so R40.6bn is not measured from R25.9bn (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p10, p24). [Open item: Skift to rebase the spend path on the FY2025 actual of R25.9bn.]

Jobs wait on the labour analysis, so the ambition of 300,000 tourism-linked jobs is tested before it becomes a target. The green-season share starts at 38.1%, but the share outside the Metro has no baseline until the data protocol delivers one in 2027 (section 5.3). Gate 1 turns the missing baselines into targets, so the first two years must produce data as well as results.
What could knock it off course

Ten of the fourteen material risks sit outside Wesgro's control, so the response to most is early warning and a route to the tier that can act. One is rated high on both likelihood and impact: restrictive bilateral air agreements and the US carrier cap. It calls for an escalation agenda with stated asks, plus route work inside existing rights.

Six are rated medium likelihood and high impact, in three pairs; first, two sit with the national tier and ACSA. Runway relief may slip past about 2033, so its milestones are tracked quarterly. Visa processing may not improve, and the escalation agenda carries it. Second, two sit in the markets. A Gulf hub disruption would cut connecting capacity, so hub work is spread across all four hubs. A downturn in the UK, Germany and the USA would hit 52% of overseas arrivals, so activation shifts towards Africa and the hub markets. Third, two sit closer to delivery. Safety incidents could deter visitors, so safety gates come before any pilot launch. A cut to Wesgro's operating budget would hit thirteen initiatives, so rand bands and a stop list are due before Gate 1.

Two more are rated high likelihood and medium impact. Climate events that close sites and routes call for a climate risk register. The loss of LTO funding, which MFMA Circular No. 131 has disrupted, calls for stable funding agreements with a development mandate. Likelihood and impact are Letsema's assessment, and Steerco reviews the register each quarter (section 4.8).
What the Board is asked to decide
Five decisions start the plan, and two recommendations pass partners the levers Wesgro does not hold.
Gate 1 is where the Board next decides. It will ask whether seats on the full routes have held, whether any pilot has met its thresholds and whether the bookability baseline exists and is moving.

Several items remain open, from page references still to confirm to the source of the 250-call cruise target and a provincial employment baseline. Each is marked in square brackets where it occurs and listed with an owner in the accompanying open-items register.
